sunscreen_info.title: Why You Should Wear Sunscreen
sunscreen_info.content:
Ultraviolet (UV) radiation is invisible energy from sunlight that affects our skin in various ways. There are three types of UV rays — UVA, UVB, and UVC — and among them, UVA and UVB reach the Earth's surface and can cause skin damage.

UVA penetrates deep into the skin and causes aging, while UVB acts on the skin's surface, leading to sunburn and inflammation. UV exposure is not just a temporary issue — over time, it can lead to serious health problems such as skin cancer and photoaging.

Sunscreen contains ingredients that absorb or reflect UV rays, helping to prevent direct UV exposure to the skin. The SPF (Sun Protection Factor) number indicates how long the product can protect your skin from UVB rays. For example, SPF 30 means it can protect your skin approximately 30 times longer than unprotected skin.

Applying sunscreen is a basic act of self-protection, much like carrying an umbrella when you go out. UV rays are still present on cloudy days, and even indoors, UV radiation coming through windows can affect your skin.

sunscreen_info.title: What Is a Safe Amount of Sun Exposure?
sunscreen_info.content:
Sunlight is one of the essential natural resources for our bodies. When exposed to UVB rays, the skin produces vitamin D, which plays a vital role in bone health, immune function, mood regulation, and various other physiological processes.

However, UV radiation has a dual nature. While moderate amounts are beneficial to health, excessive exposure can cause skin damage, aging, and even skin cancer. Scientists have proposed the concept of safe sun exposure to help find this balance.

The appropriate amount of sun exposure varies depending on individual skin type, geographic location, season, time of day, UV index (UVI), and the area of skin exposed. Generally, it is measured by the amount of exposure before the skin begins to burn. The key indicator here is the Minimal Erythemal Dose (MED).

MED refers to the minimum amount of UV energy that causes slight reddening of the skin. Exceeding this threshold results in what we commonly call a sunburn. For example, people with fair skin that burns easily have a low MED, so just 10–15 minutes of sun exposure per day may be sufficient.

The key is consistent monitoring and balance. Rather than avoiding sunlight entirely, it's important to enjoy it safely under the right conditions. Even while using sunscreen, 10–30 minutes of direct sunlight per day is recommended as an essential component of a healthy lifestyle.

sunscreen_info.title: Photoaging: UV, the Enemy of Your Skin
sunscreen_info.content:
We often assume that wrinkles, loss of skin elasticity, and dark spots are natural signs of aging. However, a significant portion of skin aging is actually caused not by time, but by sunlight — specifically ultraviolet (UV) radiation. This type of UV-induced skin aging is called photoaging.

UVA (320–400nm) penetrates deep into the dermis, damaging structural proteins like collagen and elastin. This causes the skin to lose elasticity, resulting in deep wrinkles and sagging. UVA is the primary cause of photoaging.

UVB (280–320nm) acts on the skin's surface, causing sunburn, inflammation, and pigmentation. Most cases of skin tanning from intense UV exposure are due to UVB. Over time, this can also lead to pigmentation disorders and signs of aging.

In other words, photoaging is preventable aging. By practicing simple daily habits such as using sunscreen, wearing hats, sunglasses, and parasols, and checking the UV index (UVI), you can reduce more than half of skin aging.

In particular, daily use of a broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher effectively blocks both UVA and UVB, preventing photoaging. Since UV rays are present even on cloudy days, indoors, and during short outings, sun protection should be a daily routine — not just for special occasions.

sunscreen_info.title: Which Sunscreen Is Right for My Skin?
sunscreen_info.content:
Sunscreen is the most fundamental and important skincare product for protecting your skin from UV radiation. However, not every sunscreen works well for every skin type. When choosing a sunscreen, the key is not just looking at the SPF number, but selecting a product that matches your skin type and lifestyle.

Oily skin tends to become greasy easily, and heavy sunscreens can clog pores and cause breakouts. Lightweight gel-type or water-based products are more suitable than rich cream formulas. Products labeled 'non-comedogenic' are designed not to clog pores, making them safer for acne-prone skin.

If you have dry skin that feels tight and dehydrated, choosing a sunscreen with moisturizing properties is essential. Rich cream-type sunscreens containing hydrating ingredients like hyaluronic acid, glycerin, and ceramides help retain moisture while protecting against UV-induced dryness.

For sensitive skin that reddens or itches easily, every ingredient matters. Mineral (physical) sunscreens are the safest option. Zinc oxide and titanium dioxide work by reflecting UV rays off the skin's surface, causing minimal irritation. Products free of fragrance, alcohol, and preservatives are most suitable.

Combination skin, where the T-zone is oily and the U-zone is dry, requires a balanced approach. Medium-textured lotions or milk-type sunscreens work well. Choose products that balance moisture and oil, or consider using different sunscreens for different areas of the face.

sunscreen_info.title: How Your Skin Reacts to Different UV Types
sunscreen_info.content:
Sunlight brightens our mood and helps synthesize vitamin D, among other positive effects. However, the ultraviolet (UV) radiation it contains is also the biggest factor causing various direct and indirect damage to our skin. Different types of UV rays have different wavelengths and penetration depths, and the skin reacts differently to each.

UVA has the longest wavelength among UV rays and can penetrate to the deepest layer of the skin — the dermis. It destroys collagen and elastin, causing loss of elasticity, wrinkles, sagging, and pigmentation — collectively known as photoaging. This is the biggest factor that accelerates the visible aging of skin.

UVA passes through almost unchanged even on cloudy days or through indoor glass windows, so it constantly affects your skin even when you can't see it. UVA is also the type of UV that induces tanning, and repeated exposure gradually darkens the skin, potentially leading to pigmentation disorders like melasma or age spots over time.

UVB has a shorter wavelength than UVA and primarily affects the epidermis. Exposure causes the skin to become red and hot (sunburn), and can lead to peeling and itching — acute reactions.

UVB also damages the DNA of skin cells, increasing the risk of skin cancer. Because different types of UV affect the skin differently, it is essential to choose a broad-spectrum sunscreen that can block both UVA and UVB for effective UV protection.

sunscreen_info.title: How to Apply Sunscreen Properly
sunscreen_info.content:
UV rays affect our skin not only on hot summer days but also on cloudy days and even indoors. That's why many people have started wearing sunscreen daily, but surprisingly few are applying it correctly. Sunscreen isn't a product you can simply 'put on and forget.' The timing, amount, and method of application all significantly impact skin protection.

Sunscreen doesn't work immediately upon application. It takes about 15–30 minutes for the skin to absorb it and form a UV-blocking barrier. That's why you should apply it at least 20 minutes before going outside, rather than rushing to put it on right before you leave.

Sunscreen protection ratings (SPF, PA) are measured in clinical trials using an adequate amount. If you apply too little, even an SPF 50 product may only provide SPF 10–20 level protection. For the face, the recommended amount is about two finger-lengths, or approximately 1g (about the size of a nickel).

Make sure to apply thoroughly to often-missed areas: beside the ears, along the hairline, around the nostrils, corners of the mouth, and jawline. Don't forget the neck, ears, and back of the neck.

Sunscreen sits on the skin's surface to block UV rays, but its effectiveness gradually diminishes due to sweat, sebum, and friction. Therefore, reapplication every 2–3 hours is necessary for continuous protection. For extended outdoor activities or swimming, choose water-resistant products and always reapply after contact with water.

Wearing sunscreen is not just a beauty routine — it's a science-backed form of self-care for keeping your skin healthy. Apply daily, apply enough, apply thoroughly, and reapply on time. These simple principles form the strongest shield protecting your skin from UV radiation.

sunscreen_info.title: How UV Rays Affect Your Eyes
sunscreen_info.content:
UV radiation can seriously impact eye health. Prolonged exposure increases the risk of conditions such as corneal damage, cataracts, and macular degeneration. Children and post-surgical patients are particularly vulnerable.

Regarding corneal damage, UVB irritates the corneal surface, causing pain, redness, and blurred vision. Cell damage can occur after just 1–2 hours of exposure. For cataracts, UVA denatures the proteins in the lens, accelerating cataract development. The World Health Organization (WHO) has reported that 20% of cataract cases are UV-related.

Macular degeneration damages the macula — the central part of the retina — increasing the risk of vision loss and blindness. Early symptoms are often unnoticeable, making early detection difficult.

For prevention, wearing UV-blocking sunglasses is essential. Choose products with UV400 or 99–100% UV protection, and wear them whenever you go out between 10 AM and 3 PM. Use wide-brimmed hats and parasols to reduce direct UV exposure, and adjust outdoor activity schedules to avoid peak UV hours (10 AM to 3 PM).

UV protection is essential not only for skin health but also for eye health. Protective habits should be strictly maintained, especially during summer.

sunscreen_info.title: Why the UV Index Varies by Region
sunscreen_info.content:
Regional differences in UV index are primarily caused by factors such as solar elevation angle, cloud cover, ozone layer thickness, altitude, and surface reflectivity. In particular, areas where the sun is directly overhead tend to have higher UV indices, while regions with more cloud cover or thicker ozone layers have lower UV indices.

Regarding solar elevation, the amount of UV radiation reaching the ground is greatest when the sun is directly overhead. Therefore, UV indices are highest near the equator (lower latitudes) and decrease toward higher latitudes.

Clouds have a UV-blocking effect, so UV indices tend to be lower on cloudy days. The ozone layer absorbs UV radiation, so regions with a thicker ozone layer have lower UV indices, while areas with a thinner ozone layer have higher UV indices.

Higher altitudes mean a thinner atmosphere, making it easier for UV radiation to reach the ground. This is why mountainous regions tend to have higher UV indices. As for reflectivity, surfaces like snow and water that reflect UV radiation well can increase the UV index in those areas due to reflected UV rays.

These factors work together to create different UV indices across regions. That's why it's important to check your local UV index and take appropriate sun protection measures accordingly.

sunscreen_info.title: Can UV Rays Cause Hair Loss?
sunscreen_info.content:
Scalps exposed to UV radiation are easily contaminated with sebum, sweat, and other impurities due to high temperatures. In particular, these substances can block hair follicle openings, making it difficult for sebum to drain and causing dandruff — which in severe cases can lead to hair loss. Additionally, if the scalp gets sunburned from intense sunlight, the risk of hair loss increases further due to damaged hair roots.

Strong UV rays also have negative effects on hair itself. Prolonged sun exposure causes hair to lose moisture and become dry, potentially leading to breakage or discoloration. Hair consists of three layers: the cuticle, cortex, and medulla. The melanin pigments that determine hair color are located in the cortex, and UV radiation destroys these melanin pigments, causing hair to turn yellow.

Among UV rays, UVA has strong penetrating power and can reach deep inside the hair shaft. The longer the exposure time and the higher the UVA levels, the more severe the hair discoloration.

Swimming is especially popular during summer. If you expose wet hair to direct sunlight, the salt from seawater or strong disinfectants from swimming pools can damage hair proteins.

During peak sunlight hours, wear a hat or use a parasol to protect your scalp. This is especially important at beaches and outdoor pools, where UV levels increase due to water surface reflection. However, avoid wearing hats for extended periods. If you have scalp inflammation, prolonged hat-wearing can worsen hair loss due to sweat and bacteria.

When choosing a parasol, make sure the product meets standard UV protection criteria. A proper parasol should block at least 85% of UV rays (for ribs under 650mm) or 90% or more (for ribs 650mm or longer).

Consuming adequate protein, vitamins, and minerals that support hair health is also helpful. Foods like black beans, eggs, and seaweed are particularly rich in these nutrients. While you can't apply sunscreen to your hair, using a hair essence with UV protection can be a good alternative.
